name: Resin infiltration (ICON)
lead: Resin infiltration is a micro-invasive dental treatment in which a very thin, low-viscosity resin is drawn into porous, demineralised enamel. It was developed to stop early cavities from progressing without drilling, and it has a second, cosmetic use: because the resin changes how light scatters inside the enamel, chalky white patches can look much closer to the colour of the surrounding tooth. Icon is the best-known commercial product, and the name is often used for the technique itself.[1][3]

For appearance, the treatment is used on white spot lesions that appear around orthodontic brackets after braces, on the white or cream-coloured opacities caused by dental fluorosis, and on incisors affected by molar incisor hypomineralisation (MIH). Because it removes little or no healthy enamel, it sits between simply waiting, microabrasion or bleaching on one side and bonded veneers on the other.[2][6][7] DMG, the maker of Icon, lists caries-related white spots, molar-incisor hypomineralisation, fluorosis and trauma-related enamel opacities among the indications for its Icon Vestibular product.[26]

Research includes randomised trials, several systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and a large number of registered clinical trials. Reviews describe a measurable masking effect compared with no treatment or with fluoride varnish, while also noting that the number of well-conducted randomised trials is small.[8][9]

Resin infiltration is done in a dental office. Wikipedia's enamel hypocalcification article calls it a micro-invasive treatment that seals microporosities in the enamel and offers a masking effect that can improve appearance, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registry lists trials of it on fluorosis stains, hypomineralised incisors and white spots from orthodontic treatment.[27][6][16][23]

chain: Dentist etches and dries the white spot, then applies a thin resin
Resin fills the porous enamel and is light-cured
Light scattering in the lesion changes

angle.text: People with white marks left by braces, fluorosis or hypomineralised incisors use it to even out the colour of the front teeth in one short visit. It works on the lesion itself and generally does not require drilling healthy enamel.

paras: An early enamel lesion is a region where mineral has been lost, leaving a network of microscopic pores. The pores scatter light differently from sound enamel, which is why the area looks opaque and whiter than the rest of the tooth. Resin infiltration fills that porous network with a resin of low viscosity so that it penetrates by capillary action, then hardens it with a curing light. The lesion body is then physically reinforced and its optical properties move closer to those of normal enamel.[3][4]

Dentists describe it as a step between non-operative care such as fluoride and restorative care such as a filling or veneer. A 2019 network meta-analysis of non-restorative caries treatments and a 2022 update group it among the non- and micro-invasive options intended to manage lesions while sparing tooth structure.[10][11] An encyclopedia article on tooth decay likewise describes resin infiltration as a micro-invasive intervention that slows progression of proximal decay.[1]

Orthodontic patients show higher rates of white spot lesions around fixed appliances, where plaque collects around brackets. Reviews list resin infiltration among the managements, alongside improved hygiene, fluoride and remineralising products and microabrasion.[5][12] A clinical report described masking labial white spots in this way.[2]

Dental fluorosis ranges from faint white flecks to brown staining and pitting and arises from excess fluoride intake while teeth are forming. Encyclopedia coverage lists bleaching for mild cases, microabrasion for moderate ones and composite, veneers or crowns for severe cases.[13] Resin infiltration, used on its own or combined with bleaching, is studied as a conservative option for the milder opacities on front teeth.[6][14]

Wikipedia's dental fluorosis article describes the appearance as ranging from small paper-white opaque areas in very mild cases, to up to half of the tooth surface in mild cases, to brown staining and pitting in severe cases, caused by excess fluoride intake while teeth form.[13] Resin infiltration is aimed at the milder opaque end of that spectrum; the article's listed options for mild to severe cases are bleaching, microabrasion, composite, veneers or crowns.[13] A registered 2013 trial with 80 participants compared infiltration with and without bleaching for fluorosis stains.[6]

MIH affects enamel quality in first permanent molars and incisors and is a subject of concern in paediatric dentistry, where an umbrella review of eighteen systematic reviews examined its prevalence, causes and clinical management.[15] Trials have evaluated infiltration to mask opacities on permanent incisors and to reduce sensitivity in children with enamel defects.[7][16][17]

Wikipedia's MIH article describes the opacities as ranging from white to yellow-brown, often asymmetrical with sharp borders, and reports a global prevalence of around 13 percent, with children under ten more affected than older ones. It lists etch-bleach-seal, microabrasion and composite or ceramic veneers for front teeth, and mentions clear resin or resin infiltrate to seal a lesion after etch-bleach-seal.[29] Wikipedia's enamel hypocalcification article calls resin infiltration a micro-invasive MIH treatment that seals microporosities in the enamel, may strengthen it and offers a masking effect that improves appearance.[27]

The maker's description of Icon Vestibular lists trauma-related enamel opacities alongside white spots, MIH and fluorosis, and presents the product as a minimally invasive way to treat developmental enamel opacities while keeping as much natural tooth structure as possible.[26]

DMG's site lists two Icon infiltration products, Icon Vestibular for the visible front surfaces, with the indications above, and Icon Proximal for the surfaces between teeth.[26] The company presents itself as a supplier to dentists and dental laboratories, states that about 20 percent of its workforce works in research and development and that its products are used in over 80 countries.[26] Its news items discuss how transillumination, shining light through the tooth, relates to infiltration outcomes.[26]

In general terms, as described in the cited research, the dentist prepares the lesion surface so the resin can enter the pores, applies the low-viscosity resin, and cures it with a dental light; the procedure is done in a single visit and aims to avoid drilling.[3][4][8] The 2025 randomised trial on lighting conditions and a 2025 case report on optimising the procedure for MIH lesions show that technique details continue to be studied.[19][20]

Resin infiltration sits among several options for white and discoloured enamel. Wikipedia describes tooth bleaching as peroxide-based, working by breaking pigment molecules into less pigmented ones, and notes that bleaching can temporarily demineralise enamel and make white spots more visible right after treatment, with such spots often becoming less noticeable with further applications.[28] The 2024 fluorosis meta-analysis found bleaching followed by infiltration the combination most able to bring colour differences below a perceptibility threshold.[9]

Microabrasion, which removes a thin superficial layer of enamel, is listed for moderate fluorosis and as a front-tooth option for MIH, and a registered split-mouth trial compares it directly with infiltration on early lesions.[13][24][29] Fluoride varnish and remineralising products are the non-invasive options in the 2023 network meta-analysis and in the braces trial, and veneers or composite are the restorative options for severe cases.[12][13][18]

For white spots after braces, Wikipedia's dental braces article describes plaque around appliances as almost inevitable even with good plaque control and notes that treatment typically lasts six months to two and a half years, which is the setting in which these lesions arise.[30]

A 2021 meta-analysis pooled eleven studies covering 1,834 teeth in 413 patients, nine of them randomised trials. White spots treated with resin infiltration showed a significantly larger optical improvement than untreated spots (standardised mean difference 1.24) and than spots treated with fluoride varnish, with the authors rating the evidence moderate while noting it rested on few well-conducted trials. In fluorosis, bleaching before infiltration made no significant difference to the masking effect.[8]

A 2024 meta-analysis of four publications (230 anterior teeth with fluorosis in 47 patients) found that both bleaching and resin infiltration improved appearance, with bleaching followed by infiltration the most effective combination at bringing colour differences below a perceptibility threshold of delta E 3.7. Patient satisfaction rose after treatment. The authors called for more studies and for standardised colour measurement.[9]

A randomised trial in 12 to 17 year olds in multibracket treatment compared Icon with fluoride varnish using standardised polarised photographs. Infiltrated lesions had a smaller colour difference from adjacent enamel at the first follow-up (delta E about 5.0 versus 8.4), and the improvement was still present at six months.[18] A trial of 116 permanent incisors with MIH assessed masking with laser fluorescence, spectrophotometry and cross-polarised photography.[7]
A 2025 randomised trial examined whether the lighting conditions during treatment change the result.[19] A case report discusses modifications to the procedure for MIH lesions.[20]

Early laboratory and clinical work includes a 2007 paper on resin infiltration of natural caries lesions and a 2010 randomised efficacy trial.[3][4] A randomised controlled trial of infiltrating proximal lesions followed participants for three years, and a randomised trial in primary molars followed children for two years; both concerned lesion progression rather than appearance.[21][22]

Cosmetic outcomes are examined in the meta-analyses and trials described above: a 2021 meta-analysis of white spots and fluorosis, a 2024 meta-analysis of fluorosis masking, a 2024 randomised comparison with fluoride varnish and a 2023 MIH incisor study.[7][8][9][18] A 2023 network meta-analysis compared seven therapies for white spot lesions using fluorescence and lesion-area outcomes.[12] A one-year follow-up of infiltration for fluorosis was published in 2020.[14]

Registered trials include studies of aesthetic performance on enamel lesions, 80 patients with fluorosis stains treated with infiltration with or without bleaching, MIH in children (including one registered study of hypersensitivity and satisfaction), and a split-mouth comparison with microabrasion.[23][6][16][17][24] One registered 12-month fluorosis follow-up of Icon was withdrawn.[25] Results for several registrations have not been posted.

Reviews of non-restorative treatments track adverse events as an outcome, and infiltration is generally described as a low-risk, minimally invasive procedure; the 2019 network meta-analysis specifically examined adverse events.[10] Because the resin occupies the pores rather than replacing the enamel, the treatment is aimed at the lesion itself. A registered split-mouth trial compares infiltration with microabrasion for early lesions.[24]

Long-term colour stability beyond the follow-up periods of the published trials has not been summarised in the reviews above, and the 2021 review itself notes that its conclusion rests on a small number of rigorous randomised trials.[8]

timeline.event: Paper on resin infiltration of natural caries lesions published in the Journal of Dental Research.[3]
A clinical report in Quintessence International describes masking labial enamel white spots by resin infiltration.[2]
Randomised efficacy trial of resin infiltration of caries lesions published.[4]
Three-year follow-up of a randomised trial of proximal caries infiltration published.[21]
Registered trials begin of infiltration with and without bleaching for fluorosis stains and of infiltration to arrest early decay.[6]
Registered trial of the aesthetic performance of infiltration on enamel lesions starts; a review of white spot prevention and treatment in orthodontic patients appears.[5][23]
Network meta-analysis of non-restorative caries treatments includes infiltration; a two-year randomised trial in primary molars is published.[10][22]
One-year follow-up of infiltration for dental fluorosis published in Medicina.[14]
Meta-analysis of resin infiltration for white spots and fluorosis published; umbrella review of MIH published.[8][15]
Network meta-analysis of white spot therapies and a trial on masking of MIH incisors published.[7][12]
Meta-analysis of fluorosis masking and a randomised trial against fluoride varnish during braces published.[9][18]
Randomised trial on lighting conditions and a case report on optimising MIH infiltration published; trials in children with MIH register.[19][20][17]

lore.intro: Resin infiltration is discussed mainly in dental research and by the manufacturer; the claims below pair what the maker and trials report with what reviewers say about the evidence.

claims.claim: Infiltration blends white spots into the surrounding tooth
claims.believers: The maker presents Icon as minimally invasive treatment for white spots, MIH, fluorosis and trauma opacities.[26]
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis found larger optical improvement than no treatment or fluoride varnish, with moderate-certainty evidence from few well-conducted trials.[8]

claims.believers: DMG describes the aim as preserving as much natural tooth structure as possible.[26]
claims.experts: Reviews group infiltration with non- and micro-invasive caries options meant to minimise loss of sound tooth structure.[10][11]

claims.claim: Bleaching first improves the result in fluorosis
claims.believers: Combining bleaching with infiltration is used for stronger masking.[9]
claims.experts: The 2024 meta-analysis found bleaching then infiltration most effective; the 2021 meta-analysis found no significant extra masking from prior bleaching.[8][9]

claims.claim: Infiltration works for MIH front teeth
claims.believers: Practitioners use it to mask white to yellow-brown opacities.[27][29]
claims.experts: A 116-incisor trial measured masking with several instruments, and registrations of MIH trials in children are active, but one registered fluorosis follow-up was withdrawn.[7][17][25]

claims.believers: Trials follow cases for months to years, including a 3-year proximal study.[21]
claims.experts: The 2021 review notes its conclusion rests on a small number of rigorous trials, and long-term colour stability is described as less studied.[8]

claims.believers: The maker's news items discuss transillumination and infiltration outcomes.[26]
claims.experts: A 2025 randomised trial compared outcomes under different light conditions.[19]

card.summary: A resin that seeps into white spots to arrest early lesions and blend them in; trials are many, outcomes not summarised here.
card.note: Used by dentists; long-term cosmetic outcome data are lacking.

quick.overview:
Resin infiltration fills the porous enamel of early lesions with a thin resin. Dentists use it for white spots after braces and some fluorosis or hypomineralisation marks.
It has randomised trials and many registered studies behind it.
quick.mechanism: Low-viscosity resin penetrates demineralised enamel, stabilising it and changing its light scattering so spots look closer to surrounding enamel.
quick.risks: Long-term cosmetic results were not summarised, and one registered fluorosis follow-up was withdrawn.
